chapters.title: Chapter 6: Risk, Tax and Getting Started

lessons.title: Common Mistakes Beginners Make in Commodities

children.text: Most commodity traders who blow up their accounts do not do it with one exotic mistake. They do it with a handful of ordinary ones, repeated: a position that was bigger than they realised, a stop-loss moved "just this once", a contract held too close to expiry, a tip followed without checking. The good news is that these mistakes are predictable, and every one of them has a fix you have already learned in this course. This final lesson brings them together in one place, shows what each one costs in rupees, and gives you a checklist to carry into every trade.

body.text: You do not need to be brilliant to survive in commodities. You need to avoid the same dozen mistakes that knock out most beginners, consistently, trade after trade.

children.text: Size and Leverage Mistakes
Mistake 1: Confusing the Quote With the Contract
Ritu in Bhopal sees MCX Silver at ₹1,20,000 and buys one lot of Silver, assuming she has bought 1 kg. The contract actually covers 30 kg. When silver falls ₹2,000 per kg, she expects to lose ₹2,000.

body.title: The real loss
body.prompt: One lot of MCX Silver covers 30 kg and is quoted in ₹ per kg. If silver falls by ₹2,000 per kg, what is Ritu's actual loss on one lot, in rupees? Enter the loss as a negative number.
body.explanation: Loss = minus ₹2,000 × 30 kg = minus ₹60,000, thirty times what she expected. Silver Micro, at 1 kg, would have matched her intended size.

children.text: Mistake 2: Letting Margin Decide Position Size

Margin tells you the minimum deposit the exchange needs. It says nothing about how much you can afford to lose. Traders who size by "available margin" routinely carry effective leverage of 10 times or more, which means an ordinary 5% move wipes out half their capital.
Contract Mechanics Mistakes
Mistake 3: Forgetting That Contracts Expire

Futures and options have end dates. Beginners who treat them like shares get caught by tender periods, sharply higher delivery margins, forced square-offs by their broker, or, as in April 2020, an expiring contract that behaves in ways nobody expected.

body.text: The day you open a futures or options position, write down three dates: last trading day, the start of any tender or delivery period, and the date you plan to roll or close. If you cannot find these dates, do not place the trade.

children.text: Mistake 4: Forgetting Costs Add Up

Every trade pays brokerage, exchange charges, CTT, stamp duty, GST and the bid-ask spread. Per trade these look tiny. Across a year of active trading, they become a hurdle your strategy must clear before you make a single rupee.

body.title: Annual cost drag on ₹3,00,000 capital at an illustrative ₹90 per round trip
The hurdle rate
body.prompt: A trader with ₹3,00,000 of capital completes 400 round-trip trades in a year, with total costs of ₹90 per round trip including slippage. What percentage of capital do costs consume over the year?
body.explanation: 400 × ₹90 = ₹36,000. ₹36,000 ÷ ₹3,00,000 = 12%. The strategy must earn 12% a year just to break even, before any tax.

children.text: Market Understanding Mistakes
Mistake 5: Forgetting the Rupee

MCX gold, silver, crude and base metals are dollar prices converted into rupees. If WTI crude is flat but the rupee strengthens 2%, MCX crude falls about 2%. On one Crude Oil lot at ₹6,000 per barrel, that is about ₹120 per barrel, or ₹12,000, lost without the oil market moving at all.
Mistake 6: Reading Headlines Instead of Drivers

Beginners react to "Oil surges on Middle East tension" after the move has happened. Experienced traders ask what is actually changing: supply, demand, inventories, the curve, the dollar, or just sentiment that may fade by tomorrow.

body.title: Spot the misreading
body.question: Which of these beginner conclusions is actually sound?
options: Later gold contracts are priced higher, so the market expects gold to rise
Crude has fallen 60% in six weeks, so the expiring contract is a safe bargain
MCX gold can fall even when international gold is flat, if the rupee strengthens
A ₹2 natural gas option cannot lose much money
body.explanation: MCX gold is roughly the international price × USD/INR, so a stronger rupee lowers it even when global gold is unchanged. The other three repeat classic mistakes: reading contango as a forecast, treating a crash as a floor, and ignoring the lot multiplier on option premium.

children.text: Behaviour Mistakes
Mistake 7: Moving the Stop-Loss

Dev plans a Crude Oil Mini trade with a stop ₹240 below entry, risking ₹2,400. When the price nears his stop, he moves it ₹240 lower "to give it room". It happens again. He finally exits ₹720 below entry.

body.title: The price of hope
body.prompt: Dev's Crude Oil Mini position covers 10 barrels. He exits ₹720 per barrel below his entry instead of at his planned ₹240 stop. What is his actual loss in rupees? Enter the loss as a negative number.
body.explanation: Actual loss = minus ₹720 × 10 = minus ₹7,200, three times his planned ₹2,400. A few trades like this can erase many small, disciplined wins.

children.text: Mistake 8: Averaging Down on Leverage

body.title: Show me the math: averaging down in Gold Mini

children.text: Sunil buys 1 lot of Gold Mini at ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams (₹10 per ₹1 move). Gold falls, so he buys another lot at ₹99,000 and a third at ₹98,000, lowering his average price to ₹99,000.
Position: 3 lots at an average of ₹99,000
Gold falls to ₹97,000

Compare that with a disciplined trader who held 1 lot with a stop at ₹99,000: a loss of ₹1,000 × 10 = ₹10,000. Averaging down lowered Sunil's average price, but it tripled his exposure exactly when the market was telling him he was wrong.
Mistake 9: Revenge Trading and Overtrading
After a loss, the urge to "win it back" leads to bigger positions, lower-quality setups and more trades. A daily or weekly loss limit exists precisely to break this cycle.

children.text: Compliance and Safety Mistakes
Mistake 10: Trusting Tips, Guarantees and Unregistered Operators
From NSEL's "paired contracts" to Telegram "sure-shot" calls, the pattern repeats: promised returns, urgency and someone other than a regulated exchange holding your money or making your decisions.

body.title: The one-word red flag
body.textWithBlank: Any commodity product or trading service that promises ___ returns should be treated as a red flag, because no leveraged market position can promise them.
body.explanation: Exchange-traded commodity positions have no guaranteed outcome. A promised return is either a misunderstanding of risk or a sign of mis-selling or fraud, and it usually means your money is exposed to whoever made the promise.

children.text: Mistake 11: Ignoring Agri Policy Risk

Agri contracts can face special margins, locked price limits, position curbs and outright suspension. Beginners who trade jeera or guar like gold, without checking circulars, get caught when the market itself changes the rules.
Mistake 12: Getting Tax and Filing Wrong

Reporting commodity profits as capital gains, skipping advance tax, or filing late in a loss year are expensive administrative mistakes. The last one permanently loses the right to carry that loss forward.

body.title: The costly filing mistake
body.question: Which filing mistake permanently prevents a commodity trader from carrying forward a trading loss to future years?
options: Paying advance tax a few days late
Filing the return after the due date
body.explanation: Non-speculative business losses can be carried forward for up to 8 years only if the return is filed by the due date. Late advance tax attracts interest but does not affect loss carry-forward.

children.text: Putting It All Together

body.title: Capstone: Kunal's week
body.scenario:
Kunal, a 25-year-old in Nagpur, has ₹8,00,000 in his trading account, partly as pledged shares.
Monday: He sees MCX Gold at ₹1,02,000 per 10 grams and buys 5 lots of Gold Mini, simply because his available margin allows it.
Tuesday: Gold falls ₹800. He moves his stop lower so it will not be hit.
Wednesday: Gold falls further. He buys 2 more lots "to average down".
Thursday: To make back losses, he sells 10 lots of deep out-of-the-money natural gas calls for ₹5 each, calling it "easy income".
Friday: A Telegram channel says gold will "bounce 100% sure next week", so he holds everything over the weekend. He has not checked the Gold Mini contract's expiry, and its tender period starts next Wednesday.
He also reported last year's commodity loss nowhere, because "losses don't need reporting".
body.prompt: Identify every mistake Kunal made, and for each one, state the fix from this course.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Sizing by margin: 5 Gold Mini lots at ₹1,02,000 per 10 grams are worth about ₹51,00,000, over 6 times his capital, and every ₹1,000 fall costs ₹50,000. Fix: size from 1% to 2% risk per trade using volatility, not from available margin.
2. Moving the stop: this turns a planned loss into an open-ended one. Fix: set exits before entry and never widen a stop.
3. Averaging down: adding 2 lots takes him to 7 lots worth about ₹71,00,000, nearly 9 times his capital, just as the market is proving him wrong. Fix: never add to a loser without a pre-planned rule; cut the loss.
4. Revenge trading with option selling: short deep OTM natural gas calls carry large, potentially unlimited risk, taken on for small premium while already in a drawdown. Fix: stop trading after hitting a loss limit; only sell options with experience and strict risk controls.
5. Following a tip: "100% sure" claims from an unregistered channel are a red flag. Fix: verify SEBI registration and trade only his own written plans.
6. Weekend and event risk: holding large leveraged positions over the weekend exposes him to gaps his stops cannot protect against. Fix: check the calendar; reduce or close.
7. Ignoring expiry: the Gold Mini contract enters its tender period next week, with sharply higher margins and delivery obligations. Fix: know expiry and tender dates on day one; roll or close early.
8. Concentration: all seven gold lots are the same bet, and pledged shares add correlated risk if markets fall together. Fix: measure effective leverage and total open risk across positions.
9. Tax: unreported and late-filed losses cannot be carried forward. Fix: report commodity trading as business income in ITR-3 and file by the due date.

body.title: The commodity trader's final checklist
steps: I have calculated tick value, contract value and my rupee risk for this trade.
My position size comes from my risk per trade and the contract's volatility, not from available margin.
I know the expiry date, any tender or delivery period, and my roll or exit date.
I have written my thesis, what would prove me wrong, entry, stop, target and exit rules.
I have separated the commodity view from the rupee effect.
I have checked the data calendar, weekends and, for agri, the latest circulars and price limits.
I am not moving a stop, averaging down, revenge trading or following an unverified tip.
I will record this trade in my journal and report my trading income correctly and on time.

cards.definition: Fix: calculate contract value and tick value before trading.
Fix: size from fixed risk per trade and volatility.
Fix: diary expiry and tender dates; roll or close early.
Fix: treat contango and backwardation as carry, not predictions.
Fix: separate the dollar price move from USD/INR.
Fix: realistic strikes, premium sized as a full potential loss.
Fix: exits decided before entry; no adding to losers.
Fix: verify SEBI registration; reject assured returns.
Fix: file ITR-3 by the due date to carry losses forward.

points: Most losses come from ordinary, repeated mistakes, not rare events.
Know exactly what you control: contract value, tick value and effective leverage, not just the quoted price or margin.
Respect contract mechanics: expiry, tender periods, the curve and the rupee all affect results.
Decide exits before entry, and never move stops, average down on leverage or revenge trade.
Treat guarantees, tips and unregistered operators as red flags, and check circulars for agri contracts.
Handle tax as business income, file on time, and review every trade in a journal.

body.text: You have now completed the course. You understand what commodities are, how Indian commodity derivatives work, what drives gold, silver, crude, natural gas, base metals and agri prices, how things go wrong, and how to manage risk and tax. Whether you choose to trade, hedge, or simply hold gold through an ETF, you are now making that choice with your eyes open.

This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. All names, scenarios and prices are illustrative. Commodity derivatives are leveraged and can cause losses larger than your initial margin. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a qualified chartered accountant before trading or making tax decisions.
